m2-t1.introduction: See how a page becomes eligible to appear in search, then connect customer intent to one useful destination page.

sections.title: Discovery is not a ranking guarantee
sections.explanation: Search has separate stages. A page can be discoverable but not indexed, or indexed but not competitive for a particular query.

items.label: Crawl
items.detail: A search engine discovers and fetches a URL.

items.label: Index
items.detail: It evaluates whether and how to store the page.

items.label: Rank / serve
items.detail: It selects useful results for a specific query and context.

sections.takeaway: A sitemap can help discovery. It does not guarantee indexing, ranking or traffic.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Read the intention behind the phrase
sections.explanation: A high-volume phrase may be less useful than a precise phrase that matches the offer and customer’s next action.

items.label: Informational
items.detail: “How to choose running shoes” → a helpful guide.

items.label: Commercial
items.detail: “Best running shoes for beginners” → an honest comparison.

items.label: Transactional / local
items.detail: “Buy running shoes Mysuru” → a relevant product or location page.

sections.takeaway: Inspect the actual results page; a keyword’s wording alone can hide mixed intent.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Build a shortlist before opening a spreadsheet
sections.explanation: Research starts with the customer’s language, expands it with tools and ends in a prioritised list.

items.label: Seed
items.detail: List offers, problems, localities and customer phrases.

items.label: Expand
items.detail: Use suggestions, trends and related queries.

items.label: Inspect
items.detail: Read the results and note intent and competition.

items.label: Prioritise
items.detail: Balance relevance, realistic effort and business value.

sections.takeaway: Volume and difficulty estimates are directional tool outputs, not guaranteed visitor counts.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: One intent, one main destination
sections.explanation: A keyword map prevents several near-identical pages from competing for the same task.

items.label: Phrase group
items.detail: Cluster close variations around a shared need.

items.label: Intent
items.detail: Write the question or action the searcher wants.

items.label: Target page
items.detail: Choose the page best suited to answer that need.

items.label: Priority / evidence
items.detail: Record why the page matters and where the estimate came from.

sections.takeaway: A map should include the next action for an existing page or a clearly justified new page.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Should five close keyword variants automatically become five new pages?
checkpoint.answer: No. If they express the same intent, one strong destination may serve them better. Check the results and avoid duplicating thin pages.

sections.section: 4. The keyword map: the actual deliverable

m2-t2.introduction: Think of a search result as a promise and the page as its delivery. Align the title, snippet, headings, answer and links around the same customer need.

sections.title: The title makes the first promise
sections.explanation: A descriptive title tells the searcher what the page is for. Important meaning should survive truncation.

items.label: Vague title
items.detail: “Home | Welcome” gives almost no reason to choose the result.

items.label: Specific title
items.detail: “CA Foundation Coaching in Mysuru | Weekend Batches” names the offer and context.

sections.takeaway: Character counts are a drafting aid, not a fixed ranking rule. Search engines may rewrite displayed titles.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. Title tags: the single highest-leverage 60 characters

sections.title: The snippet earns the right click
sections.explanation: A meta description previews value and the next step. It should describe the page honestly rather than stuff keywords.

items.label: Need
items.detail: Name the audience’s immediate question.

items.label: Value / proof
items.detail: Explain the useful answer or supported benefit.

items.label: Next step
items.detail: Invite an appropriate action such as viewing fees or the menu.

sections.takeaway: A meta description does not guarantee the displayed snippet; search engines may select page text instead.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Meta descriptions: your free ad copy

sections.title: A page needs an outline, not bigger fonts
sections.explanation: Headings form a navigable hierarchy. Use them to organise the answer instead of choosing a heading level only for its visual size.

items.label: H1: page purpose
items.detail: State the main subject in a clear primary heading.

items.label: H2: main questions
items.detail: Group the major parts of the customer’s task.

items.label: H3: supporting detail
items.detail: Add the subquestions inside each main part.

sections.takeaway: A clear hierarchy helps readers and assistive technology understand the page structure.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Headings: one H1, then a real hierarchy

sections.title: Answer first, then earn deeper reading
sections.explanation: An intent-matched page puts the useful answer before the long introduction.

items.label: Direct answer
items.detail: Give the fee, hours, comparison or explanation being sought.

items.label: Supporting evidence
items.detail: Add relevant proof, examples and practical detail.

items.label: Useful action
items.detail: Offer a next step that matches the page’s job.

sections.takeaway: Longer content is not automatically better. Remove anything that does not help complete the task.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 4. Content that matches intent: answer first, then explain

sections.title: Internal links are your road network
sections.explanation: A link connects the current question to the next useful answer. Descriptive anchor text explains the destination.

items.label: Fees
items.detail: Link to the cost and inclusions, not an unrelated home page.

items.label: Batch timings
items.detail: Answer the scheduling question near the relevant paragraph.

items.label: Student support
items.detail: Explain what happens after enrolment.

items.label: Enquiry
items.detail: Make the next action easy to find.

sections.takeaway: Link because the destination helps the reader, not to hit a keyword repetition target.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Does a good meta description guarantee that exact text appears in search?
checkpoint.answer: No. It is a useful suggestion. Search engines may generate a different snippet from the page, so the visible content must also answer the query clearly.

m2-t3.introduction: Separate technical discoverability from the local business experience. Use evidence to choose fixes, then verify the change.

sections.title: Technical health is a set of checks
sections.explanation: A usable page must be reachable, render properly on mobile and avoid accidental barriers to indexing.

items.label: Reachable
items.detail: Check status codes, broken links and intended redirects.

items.label: Indexable
items.detail: Review robots, noindex and canonical signals in context.

items.label: Usable
items.detail: Test mobile layout, image size and interaction speed.

items.label: Consistent
items.detail: Avoid competing URL versions and misleading structure.

sections.takeaway: Do not remove a deliberate noindex or access restriction without understanding its purpose.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Search Console closes the diagnosis loop
sections.explanation: A report is a starting point for a question, not a command to change every flagged URL.

items.label: Inspect
items.detail: Choose a specific URL or search-performance question.

items.label: Diagnose
items.detail: Compare the report with the actual page and intended behaviour.

items.label: Fix
items.detail: Apply the smallest justified change.

items.label: Recheck
items.detail: Allow for processing delay, then check the same evidence.

sections.takeaway: Ownership is required for private property data. Public checks cannot substitute for it.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Google Search Console: the free window into Google's brain

sections.title: Local discovery must match real-world reality
sections.explanation: A local profile works when the customer can trust the business details and complete the visit or enquiry.

items.label: Identity
items.detail: Use the real business name, address and phone consistently.

items.label: Relevance
items.detail: Choose accurate categories and explain actual services.

items.label: Proof
items.detail: Use genuine photos and honest customer feedback.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Keep hours, directions and contact routes current.

sections.takeaway: Never create fake reviews or a false location to try to win local visibility.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Local SEO and the Google Business Profile

sections.title: Impact and effort are different axes
sections.explanation: Use two dimensions to avoid confusing a valuable repair with an easy one. This matrix is a decision aid, not a guaranteed ranking formula.

items.label: Do first
items.detail: Fix a broken enquiry link or an accidental block on a key page.

items.label: Plan carefully
items.detail: A major mobile redesign may matter but needs time and ownership.

items.label: Batch later
items.detail: Tidy small metadata issues after critical barriers are removed.

items.label: Question the work
items.detail: Avoid expensive cosmetic changes without a clear customer benefit.

sections.takeaway: State the scoring convention. Multiplying high impact by high effort alone does not identify a quick win.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Why is a high-effort, high-impact repair not automatically the first task?
checkpoint.answer: It may require planning, access and dependencies. Fix urgent low-effort barriers first where justified, then schedule larger work with an owner and evidence.

m2-t4.introduction: See links as recommendations with context, not as points to buy. Build something worth referencing and evaluate the source behind every opportunity.

sections.title: A recommendation is more than a link count
sections.explanation: The context and usefulness of a referring page matter more than a pile of unrelated links.

items.label: Relevant reference
items.detail: A local newspaper cites your useful neighbourhood guide.

items.label: Low-value placement
items.detail: An unrelated directory sells identical links to anyone.

sections.takeaway: Third-party authority scores are estimates, not search-engine grades or a reason to buy links.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. Links are votes — but votes have different weights

sections.title: Earn attention with something useful
sections.explanation: Responsible outreach begins with a resource someone would genuinely want to share.

items.label: Make a resource
items.detail: Publish original local information, a helpful checklist or a researched guide.

items.label: Find a fit
items.detail: Choose relevant organisations, communities or publications.

items.label: Pitch the value
items.detail: Explain why the resource helps their readers.

items.label: Accept the outcome
items.detail: Editorial choice belongs to the publisher.

sections.takeaway: Do not buy ranking links or disguise a commercial placement as an independent recommendation.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Small-business authority has local routes
sections.explanation: Useful collaborations can connect the business to existing communities without a large PR budget.

items.label: Local media
items.detail: Offer a genuinely newsworthy local story or data point.

items.label: Community partners
items.detail: Share resources with organisations that serve the same audience.

items.label: Suppliers / associations
items.detail: Keep accurate legitimate business profiles.

items.label: Events / expertise
items.detail: Contribute practical expertise worth referencing.

sections.takeaway: Choose plays that make sense even if the link sends no ranking benefit.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. The small-business link plays that actually work

sections.title: Filter the opportunity before you pitch
sections.explanation: Ask about relevance, real readers, editorial quality, legitimacy and the purpose of the link.

items.label: Audience fit
items.detail: Would the site’s readers actually need your resource?

items.label: Editorial fit
items.detail: Is the content useful, original and maintained?

items.label: Legitimacy
items.detail: Is the organisation real and the placement transparent?

items.label: Value beyond SEO
items.detail: Could this send useful readers or build genuine trust?

sections.takeaway: A suspicious “guaranteed ranking” offer is not a shortcut to a credible authority plan.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Off-page reputation surrounds the website
sections.explanation: People discover and judge a business through mentions, reviews and public conversations, not only clickable backlinks.

items.label: Reviews
items.detail: Seek genuine feedback and reply constructively.

items.label: Mentions
items.detail: Keep business identity and facts consistent.

items.label: Community
items.detail: Participate helpfully rather than dropping promotional links.

items.label: Public proof
items.detail: Make claims supportable with real evidence.

sections.takeaway: Treat off-page work as reputation building, not an exercise in manipulating link totals.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Would a relevant local article still be valuable if its link did not pass ranking credit?
checkpoint.answer: Yes. It can reach real customers and provide independent context. That is a healthier reason for outreach than chasing a tool’s authority score.

m2-pb1.introduction: Use the audit as a chain from evidence to an owner-ready fix. The diagrams organise the brief; the original submission requirements and rubric remain authoritative.

sections.title: The audit is an evidence-to-action system
sections.explanation: An audit should help the owner decide what to fix, not overwhelm them with tool output.

items.label: Business context
items.detail: Start with the goal and the page’s job.

items.label: Observed finding
items.detail: Show a dated screenshot, URL or reproducible check.

items.label: Customer impact
items.detail: Explain what the finding prevents or weakens.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Write a specific fix with priority and limitations.

sections.takeaway: Do not invent private analytics or Search Console evidence when you do not have access.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Assemble the audit pack in connected parts
sections.explanation: Keep the research, page changes, technical checks and roadmap traceable to the same business.

items.label: Context + keyword map
items.detail: State the goal and map at least 15 phrases to intent and pages.

items.label: Page craft
items.detail: Show before/after work for the home page and one money page.

items.label: Technical + local
items.detail: Include specific speed, indexing and profile evidence where available.

items.label: Authority + roadmap
items.detail: Name realistic outlets and prioritised owner-ready actions.

items.label: Integrity
items.detail: Include access limits, reflection and the AI-use statement.

sections.takeaway: Use the original “What to submit” list as the final completeness checklist.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Check coverage across five evidence families
sections.explanation: A strong-looking page rewrite is not a complete audit if it skips technical or local evidence.

items.label: Indexability
items.detail: At least one finding about intended crawl or indexing behaviour.

items.label: On-page
items.detail: At least two findings with rewritten titles or descriptions.

items.label: Speed
items.detail: At least one specific opportunity, naming the relevant resource.

items.label: Local
items.detail: At least one real profile gap.

items.label: Authority
items.detail: At least one realistic recommendation with a named outlet.

sections.takeaway: Evidence can confirm that something is healthy; do not manufacture a defect just to fill a box.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Work in passes, then test the instructions
sections.explanation: A peer should be able to understand the proposed fixes without needing the author to interpret them.

items.label: Collect
items.detail: Choose the site and save dated evidence.

items.label: Analyse
items.detail: Build the keyword map and before/after changes.

items.label: Peer-test
items.detail: Ask a partner to follow the top-three instructions.

items.label: Prioritise / submit
items.detail: Finish the roadmap, limits and reflection.

sections.takeaway: Keep impact and effort definitions explicit; do not let a high-effort score accidentally masquerade as an easy win.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Professional quality is visible in the evidence
sections.explanation: The rubric values judgement and usability, not a large count of findings.

items.label: Evidence and craft
items.detail: Findings are demonstrated and rewrites match intent.

items.label: Coverage and judgement
items.detail: Technical, local and authority work are specific and prioritised.

items.label: Honesty and usability
items.detail: Limits are visible and an owner can act on the roadmap.

sections.takeaway: This is a rubric-reading aid, not a new marks scheme. Apply the published rubric and facilitator guidance.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: You cannot access the site’s Search Console. What belongs in the audit?
checkpoint.answer: State the limitation, use appropriate public evidence, and say what access would close the gap. Never fabricate a private-property screenshot or an indexing conclusion you cannot support.
